```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

When a response changes with a covariate along a curve whose shape is not known,
`semireg()` fits it as a penalized spline inside a linear or generalized linear mixed
model (Ruppert, Wand and Carroll 2003). The spline's wiggly part is a random effect, so
the amount of smoothing is estimated by REML along with the other variance components,
and the usual mixed-model tools apply. Smooths are written in the model formula, as for
`mgcv::gam()`, next to fixed and lme4 random terms. `semipred()` predicts the curves with
confidence bands; `predictmeans()` gives means and comparisons of factor levels with the
smooth included.

## Data and model

The `Dialyzer` data (package nlme) give the ultrafiltration rate of 20 dialyzers at
seven transmembrane pressures, at two blood flow rates (`QB`, 200 or 300 dl/min).

```{r}
library(predictmeans)
data(Dialyzer, package = "nlme")
Dialyzer <- as.data.frame(Dialyzer)
```

The rate rises with pressure and levels off. The model has a curve for each blood flow
rate, `s(pressure, by = QB)`, and a random intercept and slope for each dialyzer:

```{r}
fm <- semireg(rate ~ s(pressure, by = QB, bs = "os", k = 4) + (pressure | Subject),
              data = Dialyzer, prt = FALSE)
```

`bs = "os"` is the O'Sullivan penalized spline (Wand and Ormerod 2008) with `k` interior
knots; any mgcv basis can be used instead (the default is a thin plate spline). Each curve
is split into a straight line, whose terms (`QB + QB:pressure`) are added to the fixed
effects automatically, and a smooth departure from it, a block of random effects with its
own variance.

| Written | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `s(x)` | one curve |
| `s(x, by = f)` | a curve per level of `f`, a variance each (`id = 1`: one shared) |
| `s(x, by = z)`, `z` numeric | varying coefficient |
| `s(x, f)` | common curve + a deviation curve per level of `f` |
| `s(x, f1*f2)` | common curve + deviations for `f1`, `f2`, `f1:f2`, a variance each |
| `s(x1, x2)`, `s(x1, x2, bs = "ztps")` | surface |
| `t2(x1, x2)` | tensor-product surface (covariates on different scales), a variance per penalty; `te()` is fitted as `t2()` |
| `s(x, bs = "user", xt = list(basis = f))` | a basis of your own, `f(x)` (checked before the fit) |
| `(s(x, k = 10) \| g)` | random curve per subject: `(x \| g)` + a spline deviation |

`?semireg` has the full table. `anova(fm)` gives the tests of the
fixed effects (Type III, Kenward-Roger df) and, for each smooth term, the likelihood ratio
test of its variance being zero: a significant smooth term means the curve is not a
straight line.

```{r}
anova(fm)
```

## Curves with confidence bands

```{r}
cur <- semipred(fm, "QB", "pressure", prt = FALSE)
head(cur$pred_df)
cur$plt
```

The band is pointwise: at each pressure it covers the true curve with 95% probability
(`level = 0.05`). Before version 2.0 these limits were 90% limits; `level = 0.1` gives
them. They are t limits with the Satterthwaite df of each point (column `df`), from the
variance components of the design (here the dialyzers) and the residual.

A **simultaneous** band covers the whole curve at once with 95% probability, so it is
wider. Use it to judge the shape of the curve over its whole range:

```{r}
sim <- semipred(fm, "QB", "pressure", simultaneous = TRUE, prt = FALSE)
p <- sim$pred_df
head(data.frame(pressure = p$pressure, df = p$df, pointwise = qt(0.975, p$df),
                simultaneous = (p$UL - p$rate) / p$SE))
sim$plt
```

The critical values come from 10,000 draws of the estimates' distribution (a
multivariate t), with a fixed seed, so the band is the same each time.

## Where do the curves differ?

`contr` gives the difference between two curves, here 300 minus 200 dl/min, with its
band. Where a simultaneous band excludes zero, the curves differ, with the error rate
controlled over the whole range of pressures. Here the higher blood flow rate gives a
higher ultrafiltration rate from a pressure of about 1.2 upwards:

```{r}
dif <- semipred(fm, "QB", "pressure", contr = c(2, 1), simultaneous = TRUE, prt = FALSE)
dif$plt
```

## Slopes and curvature: `deriv`

`deriv = 1` gives the slope of each curve along the covariate, `deriv = 2` its
curvature, with the same bands and df. Where the band lies above zero the rate still
rises with pressure; the ranges are printed and kept in `attr(pred_df, "significant")`
(here with a simultaneous band, which holds over the whole range at once):

```{r}
slp <- semipred(fm, "QB", "pressure", deriv = 1, simultaneous = TRUE, prt = FALSE)
attr(slp$pred_df, "significant")
slp$plt
```

`contr` with `deriv` compares the slopes of two curves. The derivatives are those of the
whole fitted curve (fixed and smooth parts), for any basis, and for the O'Sullivan basis
equal the exact derivatives of `smZ(drv = )`. For generalized models they are on the link
scale. In a simulation (`dev/sim-semipred-deriv.R` in the package sources) their bands
covered the true slope and curvature 0.97-1.00 at the 95% level.

## Means of factor levels

`predictmeans()` accepts a `semireg()` fit. The means of the blood flow rates include
the smooth (as `semipred()` gives at the same pressure), at the mean pressure or at
values given by name:

```{r}
predictmeans(fm, "QB")
predictmeans(fm, "QB", covariate = c(pressure = 1))$means
```

For gaussian fits the tests are t tests with Satterthwaite df (next section), and
`semipred()` uses the same df for its bands (column `df`); generalized fits get the df of
the design's strata, as GLMMs do (normal-based when the model has no random term besides
the smooths).

## What predictmeans adds

A smoothing program (`mgcv::gam()`, gamm4) fits these models too. predictmeans adds the
mixed-model inference around them.

**Means at a covariate value in a designed experiment.** Three treatments on the whole
plots of six blocks, measured at eleven times; a curve over time for each treatment.
The treatment means at time 5 include the curves' random coefficients, and their
comparisons rest on the whole-plot variation, so they have far fewer degrees of freedom
than the 180 residual df. predictmeans gives them Satterthwaite df for the combination of
fixed and smooth coefficients (as SAS does for estimates that involve random effects),
from the variance components of the design with the smoothing parameters held at their
estimates; normal-based tests would reject a true null hypothesis too often
(`dev/sim-semireg-df.R` in the package sources), and normal bands of the curves cover
0.91 instead of 0.95 (`dev/sim-semipred-df.R`).

```{r}
set.seed(11)
sp <- expand.grid(t = 0:10, A = factor(c("a1", "a2", "a3")), Block = factor(1:6))
sp$y <- 2 + sin(sp$t/2) + c(0, 0.5, 1)[sp$A]*sp$t/10 + rnorm(6, 0, 0.5)[sp$Block] +
  rnorm(18, 0, 0.4)[interaction(sp$Block, sp$A)] + rnorm(nrow(sp), 0, 0.3)
fsp <- semireg(y ~ s(t, by = A, bs = "os", k = 6) + (1 | Block) + (1 | Block:A),
               data = sp, prt = FALSE)
pm <- predictmeans(fsp, "A", covariate = c(t = 5), pairwise = TRUE)
pm$means
pm$pairs[c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "std.error", "df", "p.value")]
```

The smooth terms are written in the formula: `s(t, by = A)` adds the fixed terms `A + A:t`
(the straight lines) itself.

**Which differences between curves are needed?** In `s(x, f1*f2)` the curves are a common
curve plus deviation curves for `f1`, `f2` and `f1:f2`, each with its own variance.
`anova()` tests each variance (the likelihood ratio against its boundary distribution, as `varcomp(fit, test = TRUE)`) and
`varcomp()` shows their sizes. Here the shapes differ by `f1` only:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
dd <- expand.grid(x = seq(0, 1, length = 25), f1 = factor(c("p", "q")),
                  f2 = factor(c("u", "v", "w")), rep = 1:4)
dd$id <- interaction(dd$f1, dd$f2, dd$rep)
dd$y <- sin(2*pi*dd$x) + (dd$f1 == "q")*1.5*sin(pi*dd$x)^2 +
  rnorm(nlevels(dd$id), 0, 0.2)[dd$id] + rnorm(nrow(dd), 0, 0.25)
fx <- semireg(y ~ s(x, f1*f2, bs = "os", k = 8) + (1 | id), data = dd, prt = FALSE)
anova(fx)$smooth[c("term", "variance", "LRT", "p.value")]
```

The test is conservative: in 200 simulated data sets like these, with no `f2` or `f1:f2`
differences, it rejected at the 5% level in 1-3% of them, and it found the `f1` difference
in all (`dev/sim-semireg-lrt.R`). `permlmer()` on `fx$semer` gives a permutation test
when a level closer to 5% matters.

**Counts: rate ratios between curves.** `semireg_tmb()` fits the same smooths with
glmmTMB, so a negative binomial with zero inflation is available. `contr` gives the
difference of two curves on the log scale and as a ratio, with a simultaneous band and the
ranges where the ratio differs from 1:

```{r}
set.seed(5)
cn <- expand.grid(x = seq(0, 3, length = 30), trt = factor(c("ctl", "trt")), site = factor(1:8))
cn$y <- rnbinom(nrow(cn), size = 3,
                mu = exp(1 + sin(cn$x) + (cn$trt == "trt")*0.5*cn$x + rnorm(8, 0, 0.3)[cn$site]))
cn$y[runif(nrow(cn)) < 0.1] <- 0
fc <- semireg_tmb(y ~ s(x, by = trt, bs = "os", k = 6) + (1 | site), ziformula = ~ 1,
                  family = glmmTMB::nbinom2, data = cn, prt = FALSE)
rr <- semipred(fc, "trt", "x", contr = c("trt", "ctl"), band = "simultaneous", prt = FALSE)
attr(rr$pred_df, "significant")
rr$plt
```

**Subject-specific curves.** `(s(age, k = 10) | idnum)` gives each subject a random
straight line, `(age | idnum)`, and a random spline deviation with one variance for all
subjects (Durban et al. 2005). The heights of 28 black boys of the Indiana growth study
(`data(growthIndiana)`), fitted as in Harezlak, Ruppert and Wand (2018, section 9.2); the
fit is the same as that of their `nlme::lme()` code:

```{r}
data(growthIndiana)
gb <- subset(growthIndiana, male == 1 & black == 1)
gb$idnum <- factor(gb$idnum)
fg <- semireg(height ~ s(age, bs = "os", k = 20, xt = list(range = c(5.5, 20))) +
                (s(age, k = 10, xt = list(range = c(5.5, 20))) | idnum), data = gb, prt = FALSE)
logLik(fg$semer)
semipred(fg, "age", "age", prt = FALSE)$plt
```

The population curve leaves out the subjects' curves; `anova(fg)` would test whether
they are needed beyond straight lines.

## More situations

Each example below is complete; the data are simulated unless named.

**Several smooths and a varying coefficient.** An additive model with a curve in `x1`, and
an effect of `z` that changes smoothly with `x2` (`by = z`, a numeric variable):

```{r}
set.seed(2)
da <- data.frame(x1 = runif(200), x2 = runif(200), z = rnorm(200))
da$y <- sin(3*da$x1) + da$z*sin(2*pi*da$x2) + rnorm(200, 0, 0.3)
fa <- semireg(y ~ s(x1, bs = "os") + s(x2, by = z, bs = "os"), data = da, prt = FALSE)
anova(fa)$smooth[c("term", "variance", "LRT", "p.value")]
semipred(fa, covariate = "x1", prt = FALSE)$plt
```

**A surface.** Copper grade over a mining area (`data(copper)`): a thin-plate surface over
the plane (`bs = "ztps"`) and a curve in depth, on the log scale, back-transformed for the
plots:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
data(copper)
fcu <- semireg(log(grade) ~ s(zcoord, bs = "os") + s(xcoord, ycoord, bs = "ztps", k = 6),
               data = copper, prt = FALSE)
semipred(fcu, covariate = c("xcoord", "ycoord"), trans = exp, prt = FALSE)$plt
```

**Binary responses.** The probability of a response over `x` for two groups, with a random
effect of cluster; `contr` gives the log odds ratio of the curves and the odds ratio:

```{r}
set.seed(4)
db <- expand.grid(x = seq(0, 1, length = 25), g = factor(c("a", "b")), cl = factor(1:12))
db$y <- rbinom(nrow(db), 1, plogis(-1 + 2*sin(pi*db$x) + 0.8*(db$g == "b")*db$x +
                                     rnorm(12, 0, 0.5)[db$cl]))
fbin <- semireg(y ~ s(x, by = g, bs = "os", k = 6) + (1 | cl), family = binomial,
                data = db, prt = FALSE)
semipred(fbin, "g", "x", prt = FALSE)$plt
head(semipred(fbin, "g", "x", contr = c("b", "a"), prt = FALSE)$pred_df[
  c("x", "odds.ratio", "odds.ratio.LL", "odds.ratio.UL")])
```

**Repeated measures with serial correlation.** Curves over time for three treatments,
twelve subjects, AR(1) correlation of the residuals within a subject (`semireg_tmb()`,
glmmTMB's `ar1()` as the residual covariance, `dispformula = ~0`); treatment means at a
time with Satterthwaite df:

```{r}
set.seed(9)
dr <- expand.grid(t = 1:8, id = factor(1:12))
dr$A <- factor(rep(c("a1", "a2", "a3"), each = 32))
dr$y <- sin(dr$t/3) + rnorm(12, 0, 0.4)[dr$id] +
  unlist(lapply(1:12, function(i) as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.6), 8, sd = 0.4))))
dr$tf <- factor(dr$t)
far <- semireg_tmb(y ~ s(t, by = A, bs = "os", k = 4) + (1 | id) + ar1(tf + 0 | id),
                   dispformula = ~0, data = dr, prt = FALSE)
predictmeans(far, "A", covariate = c(t = 4), pairwise = TRUE)$pairs[
  c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "std.error", "df", "p.value")]
```

**A tensor-product surface.** Two covariates on different scales (`data(ozoneCalif)`:
inversion base height in feet, its temperature in degrees F) call for `t2()`, whose
smoothness differs by direction; each of its penalties is a random effect with its own
variance, and `x1 + x2 + x1:x2` are added to the fixed effects:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
data(ozoneCalif)
fo <- semireg(ozone ~ t2(inversion.base.height, inversion.base.temp) +
                s(daggett.pressure.gradient, bs = "os", k = 15), data = ozoneCalif, prt = FALSE)
anova(fo)$smooth[c("term", "variance", "LRT", "p.value")]
semipred(fo, covariate = c("inversion.base.height", "inversion.base.temp"), prt = FALSE)$plt
```

**A basis of your own.** A seasonal cycle on a straight trend: two years of daily values and
a Fourier basis (`bs = "user"`, with no fixed part of its own, `null = "none"`). The basis
function is checked before the fit: it must give the same row for the same day whatever
data it is given.

```{r}
set.seed(3)
ds <- data.frame(day = 1:730)
ds$y <- 10 + 0.002*ds$day + 2*sin(2*pi*ds$day/365) + rnorm(730)
season <- function(d) cbind(sin(2*pi*d/365), cos(2*pi*d/365), sin(4*pi*d/365), cos(4*pi*d/365))
fs <- semireg(y ~ day + s(day, bs = "user", xt = list(basis = season, null = "none")),
              data = ds, prt = FALSE)
semipred(fs, covariate = "day", prt = FALSE)$plt
```

## Examples from the semiparametric regression literature

The package has the data of M. P. Wand's examples, which `semireg()` reproduces
(`tests/testthat/test-semireg-golden.R`): `growthIndiana` (above), `SBMDfem`, `ozoneCalif`,
`scallop` (with `scallopKnots` and `scallopBdry`), `wageTUnion` and `copper` (with
`copperKnots`). Their help pages have the analyses; a few here.

**Bone density by ethnic group** (`SBMDfem`): a curve over age, ethnicity as a fixed
effect and a random intercept per girl; the groups compared at age 15:

```{r}
data(SBMDfem)
SBMDfem$idnum <- factor(SBMDfem$idnum)
fsb <- semireg(spnbmd ~ s(age, bs = "os", k = 15) + ethnicity + (1 | idnum),
               data = SBMDfem, prt = FALSE)
pm_sb <- predictmeans(fsb, "ethnicity", covariate = c(age = 15), pairwise = TRUE, adj = "tukey")
pm_sb$means
```

**Scallop catches over the sea floor** (`scallop`): a thin-plate surface with the knots
of the original fit, drawn inside the boundary of the survey area on the scale of the
catch:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
data(scallop); data(scallopKnots); data(scallopBdry)
fsc <- semireg(asinh(tot.catch) ~ s(longitude, latitude, bs = "ztps",
                                   xt = list(knots = as.matrix(scallopKnots))),
               data = scallop, prt = FALSE)
semipred(fsc, covariate = c("longitude", "latitude"), boundary = scallopBdry,
         trans = sinh, prt = FALSE)$plt
```

**Union membership over the wage** (`wageTUnion`): penalised spline logistic regression,
the probability with its band:

```{r}
data(wageTUnion)
fw <- semireg(unionMember ~ s(wage, bs = "os", k = 15), family = binomial,
              data = wageTUnion, prt = FALSE)
semipred(fw, "wage", "wage", prt = FALSE)$plt
```

## From the `smoothZ` form

Code written for 1.x, with the smooths in `smoothZ = list(smZ(...))` and their straight
lines written in the formula, still runs and gives the same fits. The formula form gives
the same model and adds the fixed terms itself:

| 1.x | 2.0 |
|---|---|
| `y ~ x, smoothZ = list(sm = smZ(x, k = 10))` | `y ~ s(x, bs = "os", k = 10)` |
| `y ~ x*f, smoothZ = list(sm = smZ(x, k = 10, by = f, group = TRUE))` | `y ~ s(x, by = f, bs = "os", k = 10)` |
| `y ~ x*f, smoothZ = list(sm = smZ(x, k = 10, by = f))` | `y ~ s(x, by = f, bs = "os", k = 10, id = 1)` |
| `y ~ x1 + x2, smoothZ = list(sm = smZ(cbind(x1, x2), type = "Ztps"))` | `y ~ s(x1, x2, bs = "ztps", k = 6)` |
| `smZ(x, intKnots = kn, range.x = r)` | `s(x, bs = "os", xt = list(knots = kn, range = r))` |
| `smoothZ = list(sm = myZ(x))`, a matrix of your own | `s(x, bs = "user", xt = list(basis = myZ))` |
| `smZ(x, drv = 1)` (derivative of the basis) | `semipred(fit, ..., deriv = 1)` |

Smooths are given either in the formula or in `smoothZ`, not both. Other changes since
1.x: the optimizer is `nloptwrap` (`control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")` gives
1.x's), `semipred()` limits are 95% (1.x: 90%), `anova(fit)` replaces lmerTest, and
generalized fits include the uncertainty of the smoothing parameters in their bands.

## More

- `?semireg`, `?semipred`, `?smZ`; `semireg_tmb()` fits the same models with
  glmmTMB, which also allows negative binomial and other families.
- The worked examples on the package website use larger data sets (apartment prices,
  school scores, respiratory infections, pollen counts and a spatial smooth of copper
  grades).

subject-specific curves for longitudinal data. *Statistics in Medicine*, 24, 1153-1167.

Harezlak, J., Ruppert, D. and Wand, M. P. (2018). *Semiparametric Regression with R*.
Springer.

Ruppert, D., Wand, M. P. and Carroll, R. J. (2003). *Semiparametric Regression*.
Cambridge University Press.

Wand, M. P. and Ormerod, J. T. (2008). On semiparametric regression with O'Sullivan
penalized splines. *Australian and New Zealand Journal of Statistics*, 50, 179-198.
